facts.text: Director Gary Whitson's New Jersey studio W.A.V.E. Productions has made over 400 shot-on-video features since 1987, often letting fans script and finance their own custom horror movies.
The 2020 documentary on director Gary Whitson's W.A.V.E. Productions cost only about $10,000 to make, $9,000 of it raised on Indiegogo, and took three years. Very on-brand for W.A.V.E.
A documentary, Mail Order Murder: The Story of W.A.V.E. Productions, interviews Hayride Slaughter's Tina Krause and Debbie D about working for director Gary Whitson's no-budget horror factory.
Hayride Slaughter director Gary Whitson was a math teacher who spotted video's potential for horror in 1987, then quit the classroom to make W.A.V.E. movies full-time.
Star Tina Krause (Desire Varga) began her film career in director Gary Whitson's Sorority Slaughter (1994), a gore flick famous for its absurdly long car-washing scenes.
W.A.V.E. Productions' first title was Sisters (1988). Hayride Slaughter came out of the same New Jersey shot-on-video operation 13 years later.
Tina Krause was discovered at New York's Chiller Theatre convention and has since appeared in dozens of indie horror and erotic comedy features, earning the nickname "Indie Horror Queen."
W.A.V.E. Productions, the studio behind Hayride Slaughter, also made several films devoted entirely to women sinking in quicksand. Custom orders were a specialty.
Directors who worked for Gary Whitson's W.A.V.E. in the 1990s were astounded to learn in 2016 that their old boss was still cranking out his strange shot-on-video films.
Tina Krause also directed: her 1999 horror film Limbo was inspired by her own nightmares.
The W.A.V.E. documentary's co-director William Hellfire worked for Gary Whitson in the 90s. He says the films inspired him: 'how hard can it be' if no one expects more than mediocre?
Tina Krause says her dad got her into horror as a kid. Her favorites include The Thing, The Shining, Hereditary and the Korean revenge thriller I Saw the Devil.
One Blu-ray reviewer says about a third of Hayride Slaughter is padding: a long magic act and characters chatting in a motel room, with little murder and few actual hayrides.
Star Jim O'Rear (Clifford James) didn't just act: he also wrote and sold horror screenplays, including Hayride Slaughter itself, plus Vampyre Tales, Wolfsbayne and The Deepening.
A Letterboxd reviewer notes the film doubles as a document of a real-life haunted attraction, Frightland, with plenty of runtime spent just wandering its scares.
Before leading Hayride Slaughter, Jim O'Rear worked as a stuntman and effects artist on projects like Star Trek IV, Lethal Weapon 3 and Stephen King's The Boogeyman, according to his bio.
W.A.V.E. alumni went mainstream: Misty Mundae landed a role on Showtime's Masters of Horror after W.A.V.E.-style shoestring work.
Jim O'Rear returned as his character Clifford James in the 2003 sequel Hayride Slaughter II, where he is reportedly hellbent on revenge.
Dean Paul (Joseph Peale) also turned up in the W.A.V.E.-era titles The Necktie Strangler (2000) and The Blind Date Strangler (2003). Stranglers were a running theme.
Despite the 85-minute running time on this stream, Hayride Slaughter was listed at about 80 minutes on its June 15, 2001 US release.
Veronika Blu, the film's 1st Victim, also appeared in The Necktie Strangler (2000) and The Go-Go Girl Strangler! (2000). Her horror résumé is full of strangler titles.
W.A.V.E. Productions' Sorority Slaughter and its sequel later got a Blu-ray debut, mastered from the original S-VHS tape, from Vinegar Syndrome's Saturn's Core label.
Director Gary Whitson is still at it: he's credited on Mad Doctor of Zombie Island (2008) and Giftwrapped & Gutted (2019), nearly two decades after Hayride Slaughter.
Jim O'Rear later premiered a haunt-themed horror film, Scream Farm: The Movie, at OmegaCon, a fitting return to Halloween attractions.
Debbie D (Erica Phillips) appears at sci-fi and fantasy conventions as her comic-book alter ego 'Destiny the Vampire Mermaid,' who is featured monthly in Scary Monsters Magazine.
